title: GIN & GiST Indexes: JSONB, Arrays & Search
description: Index JSONB documents, PostgreSQL arrays, full-text search vectors, and spatial geometries using GIN and GiST.

data.text: Standard B-tree indexes are designed for scalar values with a single key per row. When indexing composite elements (such as JSONB keys, tags in an array, or words in a text document), a single row contains **multiple elements**. **GIN (Generalized Inverted Index)** maps individual elements back to rows, functioning like the index at the back of a textbook.
GIN for Full-Text Search and JSONB

data.title: Indexing Full-Text Search with GIN
data.content: Accelerating text search vectors with GIN.

data.text: Picking GIN for JSONB and Pattern Matching

GIN excels when one row contains many indexable tokens: JSONB keys, array elements, or `tsvector` lexemes. For JSONB containment you can also choose the `jsonb_path_ops` operator class, which is smaller and faster for `@>` queries but does not support key-existence operators such as `?`. For `LIKE` and `ILIKE`, a GIN index over `pg_trgm` is what makes a leading-wildcard search sargable.

data.title: GIN for JSONB containment and trigram search
data.content: The first index accelerates `@>` containment; the second makes `ILIKE '%...%'` use an index instead of a full scan.

data.title: GIN indexes are expensive to update
data.text: Because a single row can produce many index entries, GIN maintenance is heavier than B-tree and can involve a pending list that is merged on later writes (or at `gin_pending_list_limit`). The `fastupdate` storage parameter batches entries for write throughput at the cost of read latency until the list is flushed. For write-heavy tables, budget for that and tune with `VACUUM`.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: GIN indexes are ideal for multi-value columns (JSONB, Arrays, `tsvector`).
GiST indexes excel at geometric shapes, ranges, and nearest-neighbor search (`<->`).
GIN indexes are slower to update but provide blazing-fast containment searches.
